transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well… I suppose I came in because I’ve had this feeling lately—quiet, but it doesn’t really go away—that the best part of my life might already be behind me. And I know that sounds dramatic, maybe, but it’s not like I’m making some grand statement.

I’ve always been someone who could make a plan, stick to it, keep things in order—graduate school does that to you, or maybe it attracts people like that. I used to believe if I was disciplined enough I could get myself back on track. But now it feels like no amount of planning or trying hard is going to get me back to feeling like myself.
Can you tell me more about this feeling that the best part of your life might be behind you - is it a sad feeling?

Yes… sad, I suppose, though not in a crying sort of way. Most days I’m not in tears or making a scene about it. It’s more like—well, like there’s a gray film over things.

Even when I’m in the studio, where I used to lose track of time, or when I’m sitting across from my wife at dinner, talking about ordinary things… it’s still there underneath. This low tone. Like background noise you stop noticing until suddenly you realize it’s been on all day.
How long have you been experiencing this gray film or low tone feeling?

It’s been… a little over three years now. It really seemed to settle in after that hiking injury I had. Funny, I used to be very particular about my boots and routes and all that—probably overprepared, if anything—but yes, since then. About three years and three months, I’d say.
Do you find that you're still enjoying the things you used to, like being in the studio or spending time with your wife?

I’m not sure I can answer that cleanly. I mean, I still go to the studio, and I still sit with my wife, of course. Those things are still part of my life.

Whether I “enjoy” them in the same way… I don’t know. Sometimes I get caught up thinking about how I used to organize my paints, actually—there was a whole system to it, probably more elaborate than it needed to be. My wife used to tease me about that. She’s very patient with me.

But, sorry, your question was whether I still enjoy those things. I suppose I notice them, I do them, but I’m not sure I’d call it the same kind of enjoyment I remember.
Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in?

I… I’m not sure, honestly. I still do things, if that makes sense, but “pleasure” is a stronger word than I know what to do with lately.

Sometimes there are small moments—like if the light in the studio hits a canvas a certain way, or my wife laughs at something unexpectedly—but then I start thinking about whether I’m feeling it properly, which sort of ruins the thing. I suppose I notice things more than I enjoy them.

Sorry, that’s probably not a very direct answer. I don’t know that anything reliably gives me pleasure right now.
Are there any activities or things that you used to enjoy that you've completely stopped doing since you started feeling this way?

Yes… I mean, not completely stopped in the sense of becoming incapable. I still manage the basic things at home. Dishes get done, bills mostly get handled, that sort of thing.

But I’ve pulled back a lot. I used to mentor younger artists now and then, and I haven’t really kept that up. Community events too—I used to go, sometimes help organize small things, though organizing always meant I’d make far too many lists. And music gatherings… we had friends who would get together and play, nothing professional, just pleasant. I don’t really do that anymore.

Travel plans, too. My wife and I used to talk about little trips, not grand expeditions necessarily, but now they just sort of don’t happen. So I wouldn’t say my life has stopped, exactly. It’s more that my weeks have gotten… smaller.
Have you had periods where this gray film or low tone feeling went away, only to come back?

I don’t know that it really goes away, exactly. It’s not like I wake up one week and everything is bright again and then it returns. Most days I’m not in tears or anything dramatic… it’s more like there’s this low, gray tone underneath everything.

Even if I’m in the studio, or sitting across from my wife at dinner, it’s there. Sometimes I can be distracted from it for a bit—if we’re talking about something ordinary, or I’m fussing with a canvas—but then I notice it again, like background noise.

Sorry, I’m wandering a little. I guess the answer is that it doesn’t fully lift much. It just gets quieter sometimes.
Has this gray film or low tone feeling stayed the same since it started, or has it changed in intensity over the three years?

It’s… mostly been the same, I think. Not flat in a mathematical way, if that makes sense—some days it’s quieter, some days it sits closer to the surface—but it hasn’t really turned into something dramatic or disappeared either.

Most days I’m not crying or falling apart. It’s more that low gray tone under everything. Even in the studio, or at dinner with my wife, it’s there. I can be doing something perfectly ordinary and part of me is still aware of it, like a hum in another room.

I suppose over the three years it’s become more familiar, which maybe makes it harder to judge intensity. Like living near a road—you stop noticing the traffic until someone asks about the noise. But no, I wouldn’t say it has lifted in any real way.
Have you noticed any changes in your sleep since you started feeling this way?

I’m not sure I’ve noticed anything definite with sleep. I mean, sleep is one of those things I’ve never kept tidy records on—unlike receipts, which I keep far too many of, according to my wife.

But no, I can’t point to a clear change and say, “That started when the gray feeling started.” I may have ordinary older-person nights, I suppose, but I don’t know that it’s part of this. I haven’t really tracked it closely.
How has your wife described your change in behavior or mood since you started feeling this way?

She says I seem… dimmer, I suppose. Not collapsing or sobbing around the house or anything like that. More like I’m carrying a cloudy weather system with me.

She’ll notice it at dinner especially, I think. We’ll be sitting there and I’m present, I’m answering, but she can tell there’s this low gray thing running underneath. Same in the studio, actually—though she doesn’t come in there much unless she’s looking for the step stool, which somehow always ends up behind the canvases.

But yes, she’s described it as me being quieter in mood, less bright. Not dramatic, just… gray most days.
Have you ever had a period of at least a couple of months where you felt significantly better than you do now?

Not really, no. I mean, there have been better days here and there, but not a stretch of a couple of months where I thought, “Oh, I’m back to myself.”

It’s been going on since that hiking injury, a little over three years ago now—three years and, what, three months or so. Funny how I can remember that more clearly than where I put my reading glasses yesterday. But no, through that whole time, I don’t think there’s been a real long break from it.
Are there things you used to find pleasurable that you no longer enjoy at all?

I don’t know that I’d say “no longer enjoy at all.” That sounds rather absolute, doesn’t it? Like declaring a restaurant dead to you because they changed the soup.

I still do things, and sometimes they’re pleasant enough. I suppose I don’t always get the same lift from them that I used to, but “at all” is hard for me to say. Painting, for instance—well, sometimes I spend more time arranging the brushes than actually using them, which is ridiculous because I’ve had some of those brushes longer than we’ve had the sofa.

But no, I’m not sure I can point to one thing and say I used to love that and now it gives me nothing. It’s more muddled than that.
Have you had more than one episode of this low tone or gray film feeling over the past three years?

I wouldn’t really call it more than one episode, no. It’s more like one long stretch, if that makes sense.

It started after that hiking injury a little over three years ago—about three years and three months now. I remember the trail more clearly than I remember half the errands I’m supposed to run. But since then, this gray film has just sort of… stayed around, rather than coming and going in separate chapters.
Have you noticed any significant differences in how this gray film affects you now compared to when it first started?

I’m not sure I’ve noticed a clean difference, honestly. It’s not like it started as one color and then changed to another—more like the same smudge on the window that you stop seeing clearly after a while.

Some days I think, “Was it heavier at the beginning?” but then I wonder if I’m just remembering it that way because the beginning of anything stands out more. My wife says I can remember the exact brand of tent pegs we had on old trips, but not whether I bought milk, so my memory may not be the best measuring stick.

So… I don’t know. I can’t really say it’s significantly different now. It’s just been there.
Can you think of anything that you used to find pleasurable but now find you have no interest in at all?

Not “no interest at all,” no. I keep getting caught on that “at all” part.

I mean, there are things I circle less, maybe. I’ll look at the paints and think I ought to do something with them, and then somehow I’m cleaning a drawer or reading the little label on a tube of cadmium yellow like it’s a museum plaque. But if I actually start, there can still be something there.

So I can’t honestly think of something I used to enjoy that now feels completely dead to me. It’s more like the volume is turned down, not switched off.
Have you experienced two years or more of this low tone or gray film feeling?

Yes… yes, more than two years. It’s been since the hiking injury, a little over three years ago now—about three years and three months, I think. Funny, I can still picture the rocks on that trail better than I can remember what I had for lunch yesterday, but yes, the gray feeling has been around that long.
Has this low tone or gray film feeling persisted without any periods of significant improvement for the majority of the past two years?

Yes, I’d say it’s been there most of that time. It started after the hiking injury, a little over three years ago now—three years and three months, something like that.

I mean, I’m sure there were better afternoons or a decent day here and there, like when the weather turned or I got distracted by something practical, but in terms of that overall gray film lifting in any real way… no, not really. It’s mostly just been part of the background since then.
Have you ever had a period of at least two months where you felt consistently better than you do now?

Not really, no—not a solid two months. Since that hiking injury, it’s been… a little over three years now, about three years and three months, and it’s sort of all tied to that in my mind.

I mean, there have been better stretches here and there, I suppose—like when I get busy with something and don’t notice it as much—but if you mean consistently better for two months, I can’t say that’s happened.
Has this low tone or gray film feeling persisted for the majority of the past two years without any periods of significant improvement that lasted for several months?

Yes… yes, it has. I know I keep circling back to it, but it really does feel like it started with that hiking injury. That was a little over three years ago now—about three years and three months, if I’m counting right.

It’s funny, I remember the trail and the weather that day more clearly than half the things I did last week, but… yes, the gray feeling has been there for most of that time.
Has this low tone or gray film feeling been present for most of the past two years without any periods of significant improvement?

Yes, for most of it, I’d say. It’s been going on since that hiking injury—little over three years ago now, about three years and three months.

I keep remembering the trip itself, oddly enough, like where I stepped wrong and all that, but… yes, since then the gray feeling hasn’t really gone away in any meaningful stretch.
